newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmens to tender Caspian oil and gas fields.
newsitem.headline: Turkmens to tender Caspian oil and gas fields.

text.p: Turkmenistan plans to hold an international tender for the right to explore and develop its oil and gas riches on the Caspian Sea shelf, including on the disputed Kyapaz oilfield, a Turkmen official said on Wednesday.

The official, from the oil and gas industry and mineral resources ministry, declined to be identified but told Reuters the tender would be announced and held within the next few days in Houston, Texas.
"Houston was chosen to hold the tender since it was the place which hosted Turkmenistan's first presentation of its oil and gas resources in 1995," he said.
Data from U.S. geophysical company Western Atlas International puts Turkmenistan's reserves on the Caspian Sea shelf at three billion tonnes of crude oil and 4.5 trillion cubic metres of natural gas.

The official said the data from Western Atlas, which conducted seismic exploration, had already been purchased by Shell, the U.S. unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Mobil, Unocal, Amoco, Exxon, Agip SpA, the Japan National Oil Corp. and the Turkish Petroleum Company.
"Foreign companies will be offered cooperation in developing Turkmen fields, including the one known as Kyapaz which wholly belongs to Turkmenistan," the official stressed.
Kyapaz has recently become an object of discord in the Central Asian state's relations with Russia and Azerbaijan.

On July 4, Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR signed a $1 billion preliminary agreement with the Russian state oil company Rosneft and the largest oil company in Russia, LUKoil, to develop the Kyapaz field, which is estimated to hold more than 50 million tonnes of crude.
The field lies in the far south of the Caspian, between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, and both former Soviet republics consider the field theirs.

Turkmenistan, which shares the Caspian coastline with Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Iran, calls the Kyapaz field Serdar, or Leader, named after President Saparmurat Niyazov who enjoys a Soviet-era personality cult.

But on July 5, Turkmenistan's foreign ministry issued a strong protest over the Kyapaz deal. Later the government sent Azerbaijan a message on the "inadmissibility of undertaking any practical work" on the Kyapaz and nearby Chirag oilfields.
Niyazov, meeting a Russian government delegation late last month, said he was hopeful Russian President Boris Yeltsin would abolish the agreement.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov, who headed the delegation, called the Russian-Azeri deal a misunderstanding.
Last week Rosneft announced it was pulling out of the deal, although LUKoil said it would fulfil the agreement with SOCAR.
Niyazov is likely to raise the issue of Kyapaz during his talks with Yeltsin, expected to be held in Moscow on Thursday.
Much of the debate over the Caspian Sea hinges on whether it is designated a sea or lake. International boundaries would be drawn differently in each case.

Moscow has argued that the Caspian is a salt lake whose oil resources should be developed jointly by the five littoral states. Others have said that it should be viewed as a sea, and each of the five must have a separate share of the riches.
